About: a pulse let go on a long string

Source

Concept
The motion of a long string under tension after it is let go from a given shape y₀(x) with a given transverse velocity q(x) = −αv y₀′(x), where v = √(τ/μ) is the wave speed.
Serves
Fermi Notes, §3.2 Travelling Waves on a String (D’Alembert’s Solution; Figs. 36–37): a string let go from a given shape, from rest or with a given velocity, and its division into waves travelling each way.
On screen
The blue string over its baseline on fixed axes (x in units of σ, y in units of yₘ, vertical scale magnified so yₘ is drawn 6× as long as σ); at t = 0 only, thin arrows showing the velocity q = −αv y₀′ the string is given; dashed orange and purple curves that appear at the end of a run and stay until α or the shape changes; an inset that collects the two end-of-run readouts at each α. The model is an infinite, undamped string with small slopes; at 1×, vt grows by σ each second. Each velocity arrow is drawn as the distance that point would move while vt advances by ½σ at that speed (length ½σ·q/v on the y scale).
Controls
α sets the initial velocity (labels: q = +v y₀′ at α = −1, released from rest at α = 0, q = −v y₀′ at α = 1); Shape picks the Gaussian or the lopsided pulse; ▶ Play / ⏸ Pause runs the time; the time slider drags vt from 0 to 7σ, and the box beside it takes an exact vt; ⏮ Back to t = 0 returns the string to its start keeping α, the shape and the inset; Clear points empties the inset; ↻ Reset restores every default.
Readouts
In the Readouts panel in the sidebar (vt, the distance a wave has travelled, is shown by the time slider): the greatest displacement of the string on the grid x ≤ 0 (purple) and x ≥ 0 (orange), sampled every 0.01σ. A run ends and pauses at vt = 7σ.
Inquiry
Five questions and a closing summary; the student runs the string, drags the time back and reads the readouts and the inset.
Misconception
Addressed through the answer choices of the questions; no outcome is stated anywhere on screen.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honors it
Stable scaleFixed axes (−12σ to 12σ, −0.25yₘ to 1.25yₘ) at every α, shape and vt; the vertical magnification is stated on screen.
No lookup leakThe dashed curves and the inset points appear only when a run reaches vt = 7σ, the same rule in every question and in free exploration.
Operational quantitiesReadouts are measured on the string itself: the greatest y on each side of x = 0, on a fixed 0.01σ grid.
Student finds the patternThe inset has fixed axes and nothing drawn through or beside the points; the points are a measurement record kept across shapes and runs.
Honest animationThe run pauses at vt = 7σ and says the string is still moving, so the stop is not read as the string coming to rest.
Controls visibly responsiveChanging α redraws the t = 0 velocity arrows at once, before any run.
Releasing and Launching a Pulse on a String
✦Teach me
The string
End-of-run readouts against α

Guided Inquiry

1 · Released from rest

Choose the Gaussian pulse and set α = 0, so that the string is held in the pulse and let go with no velocity, then press ⏮ Back to t = 0. What does the string do when ▶ Play is pressed?

2 · Shortly after release

Keep α = 0 and let the run reach its end, so that dashed curves show the right-going and left-going parts. Drag the time back to vt = 1.0σ. What shape does the string have there?

3 · Adding a launch velocity

Keep the Gaussian and set α = 1, so that the arrows show the right-hand side of the pulse given an upward velocity and the left-hand side a downward one, q = −v y₀′. What does the string do when ▶ Play is pressed?

4 · Pulse heights in the inset

Keep the Gaussian. Run to the end at α = 0.5, and then at several other values of α between −1 and 1, so that the heights of the two pulses are marked in the inset each time. How do the marked points lie?

5 · The lopsided pulse

Choose the lopsided pulse, which is steep on its right and gentle on its left, set α = 0 and run to the end. How does the left-going pulse compare with the right-going one?

6 · What you found

A string let go from the shape y₀(x) with the velocity q = −αv y₀′ divides into two copies of that shape, y = ½(1 + α)y₀(x − vt) + ½(1 − α)y₀(x + vt). Released from rest it sends equal half-height copies both ways; at α = 1 the whole pulse travels to the right.

Each copy keeps the starting shape, even a lopsided one, and while the two overlap the string is their sum.

The Physics

Releasing and Launching a Pulse on a String · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A long string is held in a shape y0(x) and then let go, with a transverse velocity q = −αv y0′ that you choose through α. This sim draws the string at any time vt, for a Gaussian pulse or a lopsided one.

What you'll learn

  • How d’Alembert’s solution describes a string let go from a given shape.
  • What the launch velocity α changes, and what it leaves alone.
  • How to read the string, the dashed curves, the readouts and the inset.
The two held shapes, at t = 0. Vertical scale stretched, as in the sim.

What’s on screen

  • Blue curve: the string at the current vt. The axes are fixed: x from −12σ to 12σ, y from −0.25 to 1.25 ym.
  • Thin arrows, at t = 0 only: the velocity q each point is given.
  • Dashed orange and purple curves: drawn once a run has reached vt = 7σ. The sections that follow explain them.
  • Inset: after each finished run it adds the two Readouts values at that α, an orange ring for the right of x = 0 and a purple dot for the left.
  • Readouts: the greatest y on the string, left and right of x = 0, sampled every 0.01σ.
See itOpen the sim at its present settings. Watch for: the blue string at your shape, α and vt, the readouts for that string, and the inset with any points from earlier runs.

03

Released from rest, the string divides into two half-height copies

Let go from rest, the string has y(x, 0) = y0(x) and ∂y/∂t = 0. Write the motion as y = f1(x − vt) + f2(x + vt), as in the notes (3.15). The two conditions at t = 0 are:

The conditions at the instant of release (notes 3.15).

The second says f2 − f1 is a constant, which can be taken as zero. So f1 = f2 = ½y0, and the motion is the sum below (notes 3.16).

Two copies of the held shape, one going each way at speed v.

The shape divides into two pulses of the same shape and half the height. A string at rest has no velocity to favour a direction, so the division is equal. Once vt is several σ, each Readouts value is 0.50 ym and the string between the copies is flat and at rest. At the moment of release they still overlap, so the peak is their sum, 1.00 ym.

See itRelease the Gaussian from rest, with α = 0. Watch for: the hump spreading, then two pulses moving apart, and both Readouts values settling at 0.50 ym when vt reaches 7σ.
04

While the copies overlap, the string is their sum

At small vt the two copies lie on top of each other, and the string is the sum of the two dashed curves, not either one. At the centre each copy has height ½e−(vt/σ)²ym, so the string there is e−(vt/σ)²ym. At vt = 1.0σ that is e−1 = 0.37 ym, while each shoulder, near x = ±0.96σ, reads 0.51 ym.

The Gaussian released from rest, at vt = 1.0σ. The dots mark the shoulders and the centre.

The centre stays the highest point until vt = σ/√2 = 0.71σ. After that it is a shallow dip between two shoulders, which sink toward 0.50 ym as the copies part. By vt = 3σ the centre is below 0.001 ym. The notes describe a single hump while vt is below about σ; the table shows the top flattening at 0.71σ and a dip following soon after.

See itRun the Gaussian to the end, then drag vt back to 1.0σ. Watch for: two shoulders reading 0.51 ym with the centre dipping to 0.37 ym, and the dashed orange and purple curves still crossing.
05

Each copy keeps the shape, even a lopsided one

Both copies in y = ½y0(x − vt) + ½y0(x + vt) are the whole of y0, slid along the string. Neither is a half of the pulse, and neither is turned round. The sim’s lopsided pulse has the Gaussian on its right and the same Gaussian stretched to twice the width on its left, so it is steep on its right.

The lopsided pulse after a release from rest, at vt = 7σ.

The right-going copy has its steep side in front, because that is its right-hand side. The left-going copy is the same shape moved the other way, so it is steep on its right and leads with its gentle side. Each still peaks at 0.50 ym, and the Readouts show it.

See itChoose the lopsided pulse and run it to the end with α = 0. Watch for: the orange right-going pulse with its steep face in front, the purple left-going pulse with its gentle face in front, and both Readouts values at 0.50 ym.
06

A matched launch, α = 1, sends the whole pulse to the right

A wave moving toward increasing x obeys ∂y/∂t = −v ∂y/∂x. Giving the string exactly that velocity, q = −v y0′, which is α = 1, makes it a right-going wave from the start. Then the left-going copy is a constant and the right-going one is y0 less a constant; the constants cancel (notes 3.20).

The whole pulse moves without dividing.

The front of the pulse, where the slope is negative, is pushed up, and the back is pushed down. The arrows drawn at t = 0 show this. The Readouts end at 1.00 ym on the right of x = 0 and 0.00 ym on the left, and no purple dashed curve appears. The opposite velocity, q = +v y0′, which is α = −1, sends the whole pulse to the left.

The velocity arrows are drawn as the sim draws them, with length ½σ q/v.
See itSet α = 1 and look at the string at t = 0. Watch for: the thin arrows pointing up on the right-hand side of the hump and down on its left-hand side.
See itRun the Gaussian to the end with α = 1. Watch for: one orange dashed pulse of full height at x = 7σ, no purple curve, and the Readouts showing 0.00 ym left and 1.00 ym right.
07

The two heights are ½(1 ± α) and always add to the held height

The notes work out α = 0 (3.16) and α = 1 (3.20). For any α in the sim, putting q = −αv y0′ into the general solution (notes 3.18) gives the two copies below, the constants cancelling as they do in 3.20.

Right-going height ½(1 + α), left-going height ½(1 − α), both in units of ym.

They add to ym at every α, because at t = 0 the two copies must rebuild y0 (notes 3.15, first condition). The velocity only changes how the height is shared.

08

Where it matters

  • Launching a pulse. To send a pulse down a long rope or cable you shape a hump and give it a sideways shove. The shove decides how the hump is shared between the two directions. Only α = 1 gives one direction; anything less leaves a copy running back.
  • Letting go of a plucked string. A long string pulled into a hump and released is a release from rest, so it sends two half-height pulses away, until they meet an end.
Go deeper: height is not energy

A pulse of shape hy0 carries the energy τ h²∫y0′² dx, since in a travelling wave the energy per length is ε = τ f′² (notes 3.37). So the copies hold energy in proportion to the squares of their heights. Added up, the total is the E(α) below, with E0 the energy of the shape released from rest.

The extra energy, α²E0, is the kinetic energy given by the launch.

At α = 0.5 the heights are 0.75 and 0.25, and the right-going copy carries 90% of the energy. At α = 1 the right-going copy carries all of it, which is twice as much as at α = 0. The heights always add to ym, but the energy does not stay fixed.

09

Summary

In one line. The sim shows how a long string moves on after being held in a shape and let go, as you change the launch velocity α and the shape of the pulse.

Key points

  • Released from rest, the string sends two copies of y0, each half the height, apart at speed v.
  • With q = −αv y0′ the heights are ½(1 + α)ym to the right and ½(1 − α)ym to the left. They add to ym.
  • At α = 1 the whole pulse goes right; at α = −1 it goes left.

Common mix-ups

  • “The pulse splits at its peak, and each half travels at full height.” Each copy is the whole shape at half height. The Readouts end at 0.50 ym, not 1.00.
  • “The left-going pulse is the left half of the shape.” Both copies are the complete y0. The lopsided pulse stays steep on its right in both directions.
  • “A launch velocity makes the heights add to more than ym.” They add to ym at every α. At α = 0.5 that is 0.75 + 0.25.

Things to try on your own

  • Set α = −1 and work out which Readouts value falls to zero, then run it.
  • Drag vt between 0.7σ and 0.9σ at α = 0 and find where the centre stops being the highest point.
